quotes.quote: Place a barbell in a rack just below shoulder-height. Dip under the bar to put it behind the neck across the top of the back, and grip the bar with the hands wider than shoulder-width apart.

Dip under the bar and position it on top of the trapezius across the posterior deltoids. To keep the bar on the back of the shoulders, use an extended wrist grip (as when accelerating on a motorcycle) with the elbows pointed down.

Set the supports of the rack to position the bar slightly below shoulder-height. Keep the bar racked and evenly load the weight plates on each end of the bar using a collar to keep the plates in position.
Position the hands on the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width apart.
Extend the hips and knees to lift the bar off the supports then step back but stay close to the supports.
place the feet so that they are a little wider than shoulder-width apart.
The stance should be symmetrical and comfortable. Most people place the feet between hip- and shoulder-width apart with the toes slightly angled out.
Lift the chest up and squeeze the shoulder blades together to keep the straight back throughout the entire movement.
Sit back into hips and keep the back straight and the chest up, squatting down so the hips are below the knees.

Keep the abdomen flat without exaggerating the lumbar arch.

Ensure your safeties or pins are set just below your lowest squat depth. This allows you to lower the bar onto the safeties if you can't complete the lift.
Whenever possible, have a spotter when performing heavy squats.
A spotter can assist in case you struggle with the lift, reducing the need to bail entirely.

If you must bail, push the bar backward off your shoulders while moving your body forward. This will let the bar fall onto the safety bars without hitting you. Practice this movement with lighter weights to get comfortable with the process.
While the best course of action is always to have a spotter and use safety equipment, there are times when you might find yourself in a situation where you need to bail on your own.
Safeties are for emergencies; they're not supposed to be a method of training.
Proper training techniques, progressive loading, and knowing your limits are key to avoiding situations where you need to bail.
